concept.name: Online Schema Migrations

relationships.description: Connects Online Schema Migrations to database indexing in the broader engineering catalog.

concept.tagline: Altering live production tables, constraints, and indexes with zero downtime using Expand-and-Contract, lock timeouts, and shadow tables.
concept.purpose: Build a progressive mental model of online schema migrations—from why blocking DDL causes connection-pool pileups to executing zero-downtime Postgres and MySQL migrations.

spark.summary: Techniques for altering tables, indexes, and constraints on live production databases without taking downtime or blocking application reads and writes.
spark.keyTakeaway: Never run a blocking `ALTER TABLE` directly on a large table; pair the Expand-and-Contract pattern with online shadow-table tools (`gh-ost`) or Postgres lock-safe primitives (`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, `lock_timeout`).
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** Online schema migrations decouple **schema evolution** from **table locks and application downtime**.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Four-Phase Zero-Downtime Schema Evolution (1. EXPAND -> 2. BACKFILL -> 3. SWITCH & DROP); gh-ost Non-Blocking Table Migration & Atomic Swap (App (8k QPS) -> orders (Live) -> gh-ost Worker -> _orders_gho).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Choose the migration engine based on your database, replication format, and foreign-key constraints. To widen `orders.total_amount` from `INT` to `BIGINT` at 8,000 QPS, `gh-ost` creates `_orders_gho`, copies chunks in throttled 1,000-row batches while tailing the binlog as a fake.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Explore concrete migration problems covering Expand-and-Contract column renames, blue-green DB compatibility, and large-table DDL.

learningJourney.title: What are Online Schema Migrations
learningJourney.explanation: Online schema migrations decouple **schema evolution** from **table locks and application downtime**. Instead of mutating a 200M-row table in place under an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` or metadata lock (MDL), you execute changes as a backward-compatible multi-phase state transition: **Expand** (add new nullable column/table), **Backfill** (throttled chunks + dual-write), **Switch Reads** (v2 pods read new column), and **Contract** (drop old column after v1 pods drain).

sectionDiagram.title: Four-Phase Zero-Downtime Schema Evolution
sectionDiagram.summary: Both v1 and v2 application pods remain healthy throughout every phase, preserving instant rollback.

learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: understand how Online Schema Migrations works from first principles.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Online Migrations (the Lock-Queue Pileup)
learningJourney.explanation: Even a fast `ALTER TABLE` needing `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` waits behind an active 30-second reporting `SELECT`. Once that `ALTER` enters the lock queue, **every subsequent `SELECT`, `INSERT`, and `UPDATE` queues behind it**, exhausting your application's HikariCP/PgBouncer connection pool in seconds and triggering a site-wide outage.

ideas.title: PostgreSQL `lock_timeout` Fail-Fast
ideas.description: Always set `SET lock_timeout = '2000ms'` before Postgres DDL so a blocked migration aborts cleanly and retries instead of starving live traffic.

ideas.title: Replica-Lag Throttling
ideas.description: Unthrottled backfills or shadow copies saturate replica I/O; cap batches to 1,000–5,000 rows and pause automatically when `Seconds_Behind_Source` > 100 ms.

learningJourney.purpose: The problem: see what breaks without Online Migrations under real concurrency or scale.

learningJourney.title: Where Online Schema Migrations apply (and where instant DDL suffices)
learningJourney.explanation: Use multi-phase online migrations on active OLTP tables with millions of rows; skip shadow tables for empty tables or O(1) metadata-only operations.

comparison.choice: Good Candidate: Large OLTP Tables (>1M rows / >1k QPS)
benefits: Prevents metadata lock pileups and allows rolling/blue-green deploys where v1 and v2 pods share one schema.
costs: Splits a column rename or type change into 3–4 sequential PRs and requires 2x disk headroom for shadow copies.

comparison.choice: Good Candidate: Index Builds & Constraint Validation
benefits: Postgres `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and `ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID` + `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` avoid write locks.
costs: Failed `CONCURRENTLY` builds leave `INVALID` indexes that must be dropped and recreated.

comparison.choice: Avoid: Empty Tables or Postgres 11+ Constant Defaults
benefits: `ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT 0` (non-volatile) in Postgres 11+ is O(1) metadata-only (still wrap with `lock_timeout`).
costs: Running `gh-ost` on an empty table adds unnecessary operational ceremony.

learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

learningJourney.title: How Lock-Safe Postgres & MySQL Migrations are executed
learningJourney.explanation: In PostgreSQL, enforce `lock_timeout` and `statement_timeout`, build indexes `CONCURRENTLY` outside transaction blocks, and validate constraints in two steps (`NOT VALID` -> `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT`). In MySQL, use `gh-ost` (binlog-driven shadow table) with replica-lag pause thresholds.
learningJourney.purpose: Operational control: configure bounds, failure handling, and safe production defaults.

learningJourney.title: Alternatives: gh-ost vs. pt-online-schema-change vs. Native Online DDL
learningJourney.explanation: Choose the migration engine based on your database, replication format, and foreign-key constraints.

benefits: Triggerless—streams binlog events asynchronously and dynamically pauses when replica lag spikes.
costs: Requires `binlog_format=ROW` and does not natively migrate tables with incoming foreign keys.

benefits: Works without row-based binlogs and handles some foreign-key topologies.
costs: Adds synchronous `INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE` triggers on the live table, increasing write latency.

benefits: Built-in primitives handle indexes and check constraints without shadow-table 2x disk overhead.
costs: Full table rewrites (e.g., `INT` -> `BIGINT` PK) still require Expand-Contract + dual-write or logical replication cutover.

learningJourney.purpose: The trade-off: compare competing approaches across latency, consistency, and operational cost.

learningJourney.title: Production example: gh-ost Shadow Table Cutover on 120M Rows
learningJourney.explanation: To widen `orders.total_amount` from `INT` to `BIGINT` at 8,000 QPS, `gh-ost` creates `_orders_gho`, copies chunks in throttled 1,000-row batches while tailing the binlog as a fake replica, pauses if replica lag exceeds 100 ms, and executes an atomic `RENAME TABLE` cutover.

sectionDiagram.title: gh-ost Non-Blocking Table Migration & Atomic Swap
sectionDiagram.summary: Live traffic never blocks during hours of chunk copying; only the final metadata rename takes milliseconds.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why should you always run `SET lock_timeout = '2000ms'` before executing an `ALTER TABLE` on a busy PostgreSQL table?

options.text: So the DDL aborts cleanly instead of sitting in the lock queue and blocking all subsequent SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE queries
options.feedback: Correct: a waiting `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock blocks every new query behind it, exhausting connection pools in seconds.

options.text: Because `lock_timeout` automatically converts a blocking `ALTER TABLE` into a `CONCURRENTLY` operation
options.feedback: `lock_timeout` fails fast rather than changing the lock mode.

options.text: To disable WAL archiving during the migration
options.feedback: `lock_timeout` only bounds how long a statement waits to acquire a lock.

_recommendedProblem.title: Active-Active Multi-Master Split-Brain Recovery
_recommendedProblem.prompt: Redesign an active-active multi-master relational replication pipeline between us-east-1 and eu-west-1 (6,000 writes/sec, 85 ms WAN RTT, < 15 ms p99 local commit) so a 9-minute transatlantic partition and 180-250 ms NTP clock skew never cause silent Last-Write-Wins (LWW) overwrites.
